triage.name: Hydrocele
triage.reason: Common scrotal swelling that students can diagnose by history and exam (transillumination) with ultrasound to confirm, and distinguish from hernia, varicocele and tumor.

rule_errors: exam: 3 of 9 terms aren't SNOMED CT findings
review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'scrotal ultrasound with color doppler' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']

exam: term 'Scrotal tenderness' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Scrotal erythema' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Occurs at any age in males
Congenital (communicating) hydroceles are most often seen in newborns and infants
Adult hydroceles become more common with increasing age

risk_factors.text: Premature birth or low birth weight (congenital hydrocele)

chief_complaints.text: One side of my scrotum feels heavy
There's a soft lump in my scrotum

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months in adults; noticed at birth or in the first year of life in congenital cases
hpi.duration: Weeks to months in adults; present since birth or early infancy in congenital cases
hpi.progression: Slowly enlarges over time; may fluctuate in size during the day in a communicating hydrocele
hpi.quality: Soft, smooth, painless swelling; feels like a water-filled balloon
hpi.timing: Constant; may be larger after activity or at the end of the day in a communicating hydrocele
pertinent_negatives: Nausea and vomiting with the swelling

argues_against: Dysuria with fever and scrotal pain (epididymitis)
Fever and weight loss (malignancy or infection)
Groin bulge that enlarges with straining (inguinal hernia)

atypical.how_it_differs: Congenital hydrocele presents as a soft scrotal swelling noticed by parents or at newborn exam; it may be communicating and fluctuate in size, and often resolves spontaneously by 12–24 months.
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; a communicating hydrocele may be mistaken for an inguinal hernia because it changes size with crying or straining.
More often secondary to another process such as heart failure, nephrotic syndrome or a testicular tumor, so the swelling may be bilateral or accompanied by signs of the underlying disease.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; normal gait and activity
general.moderate: Mild discomfort with movement or prolonged standing; otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Noticeable discomfort, walks cautiously, may hold or support the scrotum
general.critical: Not applicable; hydrocele is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scrotum with the patient standing and supine
findings.finding: Unilateral or bilateral scrotal swelling, smooth and rounded

findings.maneuver: Shine a penlight through the scrotum in a darkened room
findings.finding: Transmission of light visible through the swelling, confirming fluid
findings.term: Transmission of light visible through swelling of scrotum

findings.maneuver: Palpate the scrotal contents, identifying the testis and epididymis
findings.finding: Testis is palpable separately from the fluid collection

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal canal and ask the patient to cough or strain
findings.finding: No inguinal bulge or impulse with coughing

findings.maneuver: Palpate the spermatic cord with the patient standing and performing Valsalva
findings.finding: No worm-like or bag-of-worms texture of the pampiniform plexus

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for any scrotal swelling or mass

findings.text: Anechoic fluid collection surrounding the testis within the tunica vaginalis
Normal testis and epididymis with preserved arterial flow on Doppler
Simple hydrocele: no septations, no internal echoes, no solid component
Complex hydrocele with internal echoes, septations or wall thickening suggesting hemorrhage, infection or tumor
Testis not separately visualized from the fluid collection

imaging.preferred_when: Bilateral hydrocele or suspected secondary cause such as heart failure, nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis

findings.text: Ascites or other signs of the underlying systemic process

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected retroperitoneal or pelvic mass, lymphadenopathy or metastatic testicular tumor

findings.text: Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or a primary mass

initial.why: Confirms a fluid collection, shows whether the testis is normal, and rules out torsion, tumor, hernia and varicocele

supporting.why: Looks for urinary infection when epididymitis or orchitis is being considered
supporting.only_if: dysuria, fever or scrotal pain suggests infection

supporting.why: Leukocytosis supports an infectious cause rather than a simple hydrocele
supporting.only_if: fever or scrotal tenderness suggests epididymitis or orchitis

supporting.why: Inflammatory marker that rises with epididymitis or orchitis
Screens for ascites or a systemic cause of bilateral hydrocele
supporting.only_if: bilateral hydrocele or signs of heart failure, nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis

not_indicated.why: Does not show a hydrocele and rarely changes management

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for an uncomplicated hydrocele; reserved for suspected tumor or lymphadenopathy
not_indicated.only_if: a testicular or retroperitoneal mass is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not relevant in a male patient

decision_points: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler is the key test: absent or reduced testicular flow points to torsion and is a surgical emergency
A soft, transilluminating, non-tender scrotal swelling with a palpable normal testis supports a simple hydrocele
A communicating hydrocele in an infant may need surgical referral if it persists beyond 12–24 months or is associated with a hernia
Bilateral or rapidly enlarging hydroceles warrant evaluation for a systemic cause or tumor

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: Both cause a scrotal or groin bulge; a communicating hydrocele and a hernia can look identical in an infant.
differential.trigger: A bulge that enlarges with crying, coughing or straining and reduces when lying down, especially with vomiting or abdominal pain.

history: Bulge appears with straining, coughing or crying and reduces at rest
Groin or abdominal discomfort with lifting
Vomiting or abdominal pain if incarcerated
exam: Palpable inguinal bulge or impulse with cough
Bowel sounds may be heard over the swelling
Does not transilluminate (unless it contains fluid-rich bowel)
Tender, irreducible, firm swelling if incarcerated
labs: Leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers if strangulated
imaging: Ultrasound shows bowel or omentum in the inguinal canal or scrotum
Valsalva maneuver demonstrates the hernia sac

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute scrotal swelling and pain; a hydrocele can develop after torsion, and both present with a swollen scrotum.
differential.trigger: Sudden severe testicular pain with nausea and vomiting, high-riding testis, or absent cremasteric reflex.

history: Sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain
Nausea and vomiting at onset
Prior similar episodes that resolved spontaneously
exam: High-riding, transversely oriented testis
Absent cremasteric reflex
Extreme tenderness, often with a reactive hydrocele
No relief with scrotal support
labs: No specific lab findings; diagnosis is clinical and imaging-based
imaging: Color Doppler ultrasound shows absent or reduced testicular blood flow

differential.name: Epididymitis or orchitis
differential.why_considered: Scrotal pain and swelling with a reactive hydrocele; infection is a common secondary cause of hydrocele.

history: Gradual onset of scrotal pain over hours to days
Dysuria, frequency or urethral discharge
Fever and chills
Sexually transmitted infection risk or recent urinary instrumentation
exam: Tender, indurated epididymis, often with a palpable swelling posterior to the testis
Scrotal erythema and warmth
Positive Prehn sign (relief with elevation) is unreliable
Urethral discharge may be present
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia or gonorrhea
imaging: Ultrasound shows an enlarged, hyperemic epididymis with increased Doppler flow

differential.name: Varicocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling and heaviness, often described as a bag of worms; common in young men.

history: Dull ache or heaviness, worse with standing and at the end of the day
Relieved by lying down
May be associated with infertility
exam: Worm-like or bag-of-worms texture of the pampiniform plexus
More prominent with standing and Valsalva
Does not transilluminate
Left side most common; isolated right-sided varicocele suggests retroperitoneal mass
labs: Semen analysis may show abnormal parameters
imaging: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler shows dilated veins greater than 2–3 mm that reverse flow with Valsalva

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: Painless scrotal mass or swelling; a hydrocele can be secondary to a tumor and may obscure it.
differential.trigger: A firm, non-transilluminating mass, a hydrocele that does not resolve or enlarges rapidly, or a history of undescended testis.

history: Painless firm testicular mass or heaviness
History of undescended testis
Weight loss, back pain or abdominal mass if metastatic
exam: Firm, irregular, non-tender mass within or replacing the testis
Does not transilluminate
May have supraclavicular or abdominal lymphadenopathy
imaging: Ultrasound shows a solid, hypoechoic intratesticular mass with internal vascularity
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging if malignancy suspected

differential.name: Spermatocele
differential.why_considered: Painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates, similar to a hydrocele.

history: Painless, slowly enlarging swelling
Located above and behind the testis
exam: Cystic, transilluminating mass distinct from the testis
Usually located at the head of the epididymis
imaging: Ultrasound shows a cystic structure separate from the testis, often with low-level internal echoes

differential.name: Testicular trauma with hematocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling and pain after injury; blood in the tunica vaginalis can mimic a hydrocele.

history: Recent scrotal trauma
Sudden pain and swelling after injury
exam: Ecchymosis and tenderness
Swelling may not transilluminate if bloody
imaging: Ultrasound shows a complex fluid collection with internal echoes, septations or a testicular rupture

severity.mild: Small, painless, unilateral scrotal swelling; no discomfort, normal activity, normal testis on exam and ultrasound.
severity.moderate: Larger swelling causing heaviness or mild discomfort with activity or prolonged standing; may interfere with daily activities but no systemic symptoms.
severity.severe: Marked swelling causing significant discomfort, difficulty walking or sitting, and cosmetic concern; may be bilateral or associated with an underlying systemic condition.
severity.critical: Not applicable; an uncomplicated hydrocele is not life-threatening. Critical illness would indicate a different diagnosis such as testicular torsion, incarcerated hernia or sepsis.

red_flags.meaning: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise; requires immediate surgical evaluation.
Epididymitis or orchitis; may require antibiotics and further workup.

red_flags.finding: Irreducible, tender scrotal or inguinal swelling with vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia; surgical emergency.
Testicular cancer until proven otherwise; needs urgent urology referral and tumor markers.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly enlarging hydrocele or new bilateral hydrocele
red_flags.meaning: May indicate an underlying tumor, infection or systemic disease such as heart failure or nephrotic syndrome.

complications.name: Hemorrhage into the hydrocele (hematocele)
clues: Sudden increase in size and pain
Ultrasound shows internal echoes or septations

complications.name: Rupture or trauma to a large hydrocele
clues: Trauma to a large scrotal swelling
Sudden pain and resolution of swelling

special_populations.differences: Congenital (communicating) hydrocele is common and often resolves spontaneously by 12–24 months. Persistence beyond that or association with an inguinal hernia warrants surgical referral.
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally. A communicating hydrocele may fluctuate in size with crying or straining and can be mistaken for a hernia.
More likely to be secondary to another process such as heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis or a testicular tumor; bilateral hydroceles should prompt evaluation for a systemic cause.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the swelling, and has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months in adults; present since birth or early infancy in congenital cases; slow enlargement rather than sudden change

key_questions.question: Does the swelling change size during the day, or with crying, straining or activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluctuation in size suggests a communicating hydrocele (or a hernia); constant size suggests a simple non-communicating hydrocele

key_questions.question: Is the swelling painful, or does it just feel heavy?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless or mildly uncomfortable heaviness; severe pain points to torsion, epididymitis or strangulated hernia

key_questions.question: Did the pain or swelling come on suddenly and severely?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden severe testicular pain suggests testicular torsion, a surgical emergency, not a simple hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, burning with urination, or discharge from the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in simple hydrocele; present suggests epididymitis or orchitis as the cause of a reactive hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you had any injury to the scrotum or groin?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent trauma suggests a hematocele or testicular rupture rather than a simple hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you had any groin or scrotal surgery, such as a hernia repair?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent inguinal or scrotal surgery is a risk factor for a secondary hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any bulging in the groin that gets bigger when you cough, strain or lift?
key_questions.looking_for: A bulge that enlarges with straining suggests an inguinal hernia, which can mimic or accompany a communicating hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, night sweats, or back or abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in simple hydrocele; present raises concern for testicular cancer or another systemic cause

key_questions.question: Do you have any long-standing illness such as heart failure, kidney disease or liver disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Heart failure, nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis can cause bilateral hydroceles through fluid overload or ascites

key_questions.question: Is there any history of an undescended testis, or testicular problems in the family?
key_questions.looking_for: History of undescended testis raises the risk of testicular cancer, which can present with a secondary hydrocele

reasoning_points: Painless or minimally uncomfortable scrotal swelling that develops gradually over weeks to months
Soft, smooth, cystic swelling that transilluminates with a penlight in a darkened room
The testis is palpable separately from the fluid collection and is not tender
No fever, dysuria, urethral discharge, scrotal erythema or warmth to suggest infection
No inguinal bulge or impulse with coughing, arguing against an inguinal hernia
No worm-like pampiniform plexus on Valsalva, arguing against a varicocele
Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler confirms an anechoic fluid collection around a normal testis with preserved blood flow
Sudden severe pain, a firm non-transilluminating mass, or a rapidly enlarging or bilateral hydrocele should prompt evaluation for torsion, tumor or a systemic cause

easy: Adult with a gradually enlarging, painless unilateral scrotal swelling
Soft, cystic, non-tender swelling that clearly transilluminates
Testis palpable separately from the fluid and normal on ultrasound
No fever, dysuria or scrotal erythema
medium: Infant with a scrotal swelling that fluctuates in size with crying, raising concern for a communicating hydrocele versus a hernia
Older adult with a bilateral hydrocele and signs of heart failure or nephrotic syndrome
Patient with mild scrotal discomfort and a reactive hydrocele from recent epididymitis
Hydrocele after recent inguinal hernia repair or scrotal surgery
hard: Large hydrocele that obscures the testis, making it difficult to exclude an underlying tumor
Complex hydrocele with internal echoes or septations suggesting hemorrhage, infection or malignancy
Young man with a hydrocele and a history of undescended testis, requiring tumor markers and imaging
Scrotal swelling with equivocal transillumination where hernia, varicocele and tumor all remain in the differential
